statement: Lecture agenda: Instagram's year-1 architecture, how a CDN works, uploading photos at scale, and a hashtag service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda: - Instagram's Year 1 archikchere - How CDN works ? - Uploading photos at scale - HashTag Service

statement: Instagram's first-year architecture: Nginx in front of Django, with Celery for background work; data in Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Memcached, Redis and RabbitMQ.
detail: Board spells PostgreSQL as 'Poslgresal' and RabbitMQ is cut off as 'Rabbit'. Both Django and Celery connect to every store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Nginx Django Celery Cassandra Poslgresal Memcached Redis Rabbit

statement: Facebook made the PHP + MySQL stack famous and everyone copied it; Instagram made its year-1 architecture famous and everyone is now copying that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Facebook made PHP MySQL famous .... everyone did that / Instagram made above arch famous .... everyone is doing it

statement: Why Instagram's architecture became famous: built in 1 year, reached 14 million users, with 3 engineers.
detail: The board does not say what the 14 million counts; audio context needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why famous ? 1 year, 14 million, 3 engineers

statement: A CDN sits transparently between the user and the origin server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN transparently sits b/w your user and the origin

statement: The origin can serve any kind of response through the CDN path: JSON, bytes, images, HTML, video, anything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: and there is a path that returns some response JSON, Bytes, Image, HTML, Video, anything

statement: Running example: origin https://arpitbhayani.me serving the path /system-design/logo.png; the CDN has its own domain, e.g. https://a.mycdn.net.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: https://arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png CDN has its own domain, say https:// a.mycdn.net

statement: CDN request flow: the user hits the CDN URL (a.mycdn.net + path); the CDN finds the origin configured for a.mycdn.net, forwards the request to the origin with the same path, caches the response and returns it.
detail: Board writes the path as 'syskm-design' [sic, system-design]. Forwarded URL: https://arpitbhayani.me/syskm-design/logo.png; purple aside 'caches it and returns'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User hitting : https://a.mycdn.net/syskm-design/logo.png goes to CDN, which finds Origin for a.mycdn.net it then forwards request to

statement: Demo: the same image is served at the origin URL https://arpitbhayani.me/static/img/arpit.png and through the CDN subdomain https://edge.arpitbhayani.me/img/arpit.png.
detail: Browser screen share, not handwriting. The edge subdomain maps /img/ to the origin's /static/img/.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: https://arpitbhayani.me/static/img/arpit.png ... https://edge.arpitbhayani.me/img/arpit.png

statement: Requirement for the image upload service: 5 million photo uploads per day.

verbatim: Requirements: - 5m photos upload per day

statement: Brainstorm dimensions for the image upload service: storage, data flow, separation of concern, privacy, extensibility, optimization.
speaker: teacher

statement: Photo uploads should not go through your API server.

statement: Object storage such as S3/GCS is cheap, so photos are stored there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3/GCS cheap

statement: Routing uploads through the API server is a bandwidth concern; instead the client uploads with a presigned URL that has an expiration.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bandwidth concern Presigned URL with expiration

statement: Step 1 of upload ('prepare'): the client talks to the image upload service and gets a random id r.id; the photo will live at s3://img/<r.id>.png.

statement: Publishing: the user keeps the random image id returned by the Image Service and uses it to create the entry in the posts table.

verbatim: User keeps track of the random image id it got from Image Svc It uses this to create the entry in posts table

statement: Posts table: id (from an id generator), user_id (author of the post), image_id (random photo id from the Image Service), caption.

verbatim: posts id → id generator user_id → auther of post image_id → random photo id from Image Svc caption

verbatim: * LinkedIn also does this * CDNs also do this

statement: Upload flow: user A talks to the Image Service to prepare for upload; the Image Service generates a random image ID and talks to S3; A uploads the photo directly to S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. user A talks to Image Service to prepare for upload 2. Image Service generates a random image ID and talks to S3

statement: Viewers load photos from the CDN (e.g. https://instacdn.net/123/abc.jpg), and the CDN pulls from S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: https://instacdn.net/123/abc.jpg CDN S3

statement: The Posts service can also validate that the image_id provided in the request belongs to the same user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Posts service can also validate that the image_id provided in the request belongs to the same user or not.

statement: When a post is published, Posts Service writes to MySQL; events reach Kafka (directly and via CDC from MySQL) and other services (search, notification, analytics) consume them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Posts Service MySQL CDC Kafka Other Services Search, Notification, Analytics

statement: The partition key on the post-events Kafka topic would be user_id.

verbatim: Overall Flow: user A uploads photo using Image Service user A posts the photo user B visits A's profile GET /users/A/posts

statement: Hashtag counts are updated asynchronously: posts are pushed to a queue and a consumer batches updates into the hashtag DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: posts → [queue] → [consumer] Batching → DB

statement: The post-events Kafka is partitioned by user_id, so it cannot be used directly to batch counts per hashtag.
detail: Live: queue label 'hashtag' replaced by green 'user_id' (02:10:00). Notes: challenge line.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: challenge : POST_PUBLISH topic is partitioned by post_id or user_id

detail: Third tag written '#nolne'; audio says nature; notes page writes '#nature'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: p1: #sunset #sun #nolne

statement: For batching and counting to work we need one event per hashtag: a post with 8 hashtags needs 8 events so we can count and batch efficiently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But for our batching and counting to work, we need an event per hashtag.

statement: Adapter: read POST_PUBLISH events from Kafka, extract all hashtags from the post, and create n new events on topic POST_HASHTAG (one per hashtag), partitioned by hashtag.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, we have to write an adapter that - reads POST_PUBLISH events from kafka - extracts all hashtags ... - creates 'n' new events

statement: Hashtag extraction re-publishes post_1729's #sunset, #sun, #nature as separate events on POST_HASHTAG, partitioned by hashtag (repartitioning and reindexing).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: post_1729: #sunset #sun #nature Topic: POST_HASHTAG partitioned by hashtag Repartitioning and reindexing

statement: Number of consumers equals number of partitions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: #consumers = # partitions

statement: Counting servers batch and partially update the count per hashtag (count += n instead of count++).
detail: Live 'Count +=n' near the DB, notes 'Batch and partially update [per hashtag]'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Batch and partially update [per hashtag] Count +=n

statement: Events on POST_HASHTAG are (hashtag, post) tuples <h1, p1>; a counting server keeps a map { h1: int } before writing.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: <h1, p1> { h1: int }

statement: The data-science (popularity) service publishes per-hashtag popular photos to its own Kafka; our workers consume it and write the top photos into the hashtag DB. It is not high throughput.
detail: Live: 'DS' stick figure -> pipe -> consumer -> hashtag DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Popularity Svc per hashtag popular photos Their Kafka * Not high throughput Workers

statement: Final hashtag architecture: Post Svc -> Kafka -> HashTag Extraction -> POST_HASHTAG -> Counting Servers -> partitioned DB; Popularity Svc -> Their Kafka -> Workers -> DB; user GET /hashtag/<tag> -> CDN -> HashTag API -> partitioned DB, with a cache.
detail: The printed box read 'Image Service'; the teacher overwrote it with 'Post Svc' at 02:23:30.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Post Svc Kafka HashTag Extraction POST_HASHTAG Counting Servers Partitioned DB GET /hastag/<tag> CDN HashTag API Cache

statement: Key takeaways of the hashtag design: Kafka as a glue, adapter pattern, effective batching and counting, read and write path optimizations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key Takeaways: - Kafka as a glue - Adapter pattern - Effective batching and counting - READ and WRITE path optimizations

statement: Hashtag reads are key-value access: for a key (hashtag) get the value (details), served from a partitioned DB such as MySQL, MongoDB or DDB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key value based access For a key (hashtag) get the value (details) Partitioned DB MySQL, MongoDB, DDB

statement: A good way to optimize systems is to identify the read path and the write path and optimize them independently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A good way to optimize systems is to identify the READ PATH and WRITE PATH and optimize them indepenc

statement: Write path optimization starts with ingestion into Kafka; the storage must support partial updates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WRITE PATH Optimization - Ingestion in kafka Requirements from storage ? - Partial updates

statement: For large-volume counting: batching, then partitioning; HashTag API servers do not count, worker nodes batch and update.
detail: Start of the first line is cut off at the page edge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: counting : Batching → Partitioning HashTag API servers won't count. worker nodes batch and update

statement: Read path optimizations: a centralized cache, the Hashtag API doing the bare minimum work, and a DB able to handle the reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: READ PATH optimizations: - Centralized cache - Hashtag API to do bare minimum work ✓ - DB should be able to handle reads ✓

statement: Key requirement is superfast response: one request /hashtag/<tag> returns a document with tag, total_photos and top_photos; everything must be returned in a single response and be pre-computed and pre-evaluated. This is the core of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key requirement: Superfast response times One request /hashtag/<tag> 1. returned in a single response 2 pre-compuked and pre-evaluakd CORE of our system
